3.title: The Household of God
3.overview:
Paul sets out who may lead God’s household. Overseers (elders) must be men of proven character: faithful in marriage, self-controlled, hospitable, gentle, not lovers of money, managing their homes well, mature in faith and respected by outsiders. Only one requirement is a skill: “able to teach”. Deacons, who serve rather than teach, must meet the same standard of character and be tested first.

Then Paul says why it matters. The church is the household of the living God, the pillar that holds up the truth for the world to see. And the truth it holds up is Christ himself, sung in an early hymn: “manifested in the flesh, vindicated by the Spirit … taken up in glory.” The rules about wine and money exist so that the pillar stands straight.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul calls the work of an overseer, or elder, a good and worthy aim, and lists what such a man must be. His life must give no grounds for accusation: faithful to his wife, clear-headed, disciplined, respected, welcoming, and able to teach. He must not drink too much, be violent or quarrelsome, or love money, but be gentle. He must lead his own family well, with children who respect him, because a man who cannot care for his own home cannot care for God’s church. He should not be a new believer, lest pride trip him up as it did the devil, and outsiders should think well of him.
verseByVerse.theology:
Character, Not Competence

Of some fifteen requirements only one — ‘able to teach’ — is a skill; everything else concerns what a man is, and the vices named are the kind a congregation cannot see for years.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: ‘Overseer’ and ‘elder’ name one office (Acts 20:17, 28; Titus 1:5-7).

Now: Verse 7 gives outsiders a say: what would your neighbours say about you if the subject came up?

verseByVerse.quote: The saying is trustworthy: If anyone aspires to the office of overseer, he desires a noble task.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The saying is trustworthy: If anyone aspires to the office of overseer, he desires a noble task.

Meaning first. 1 Timothy 3 sets out who may lead the church. False teachers had arisen, probably including some of the elders themselves (Acts 20:30), so the church needed to know what a true leader looks like. Paul describes two offices. First, the overseer or elder (vv. 1–7): a noble work to desire, but one requiring a proven character. He must be above reproach, faithful in marriage, self-controlled, hospitable, able to teach, gentle rather than violent or quarrelsome, free from love of money, a good manager of his own household, not a new convert, and well regarded by outsiders. Second, deacons (vv. 8–13): servants of the church’s practical needs, who must likewise be serious, honest, sober, free from greed, sound in the faith, and tested before they serve; the women associated with them (either their wives or women deacons) must be similarly trustworthy. Then Paul explains why all this matters (vv. 14–16): the church is God’s household, the pillar and support of the truth, and that truth is the great mystery of godliness, summed up in an early hymn about Christ, from his incarnation to his ascension.

Setting and background. In the New Testament, “overseer” (episkopos, from which comes “bishop” and “episcopal”) and “elder” (presbyteros, from which comes “presbyter” and “Presbyterian”) appear to be two names for the same office. Paul calls the elders of Ephesus “overseers” (Acts 20:17, 28), and Titus 1:5–7 uses the two words interchangeably. “Elder” stresses maturity and dignity; “overseer” stresses the function of watching over the flock. Churches were led by a plurality of elders, not a single ruler (Acts 14:23; Philippians 1:1; James 5:14). The later system of one bishop over several churches developed in the second century.

The saying is trustworthy. Key words. The second of the five “trustworthy sayings” (1:15). It may refer to what follows (the nobility of the office) or, less likely, back to 2:15. Most take it as introducing verse 1.

If anyone aspires to the office of overseer. Key words. “Aspires” (oregō, reaches out for, stretches toward). “Office of overseer” (episkopē, oversight, the work of supervising). It is right to desire this work; it is not pride to want to serve as an elder, provided the motive is to serve Christ and his people.

He desires a noble task. Key words. “Desires” (epithymeō, sets his heart on, longs for). “Noble” (kalos, good, fine, excellent). “Task” (ergon, work). Note: a work, not a title or a status. Eldership is hard labour (5:17; 1 Thessalonians 5:12), not honour for its own sake. In a culture where church leadership brought danger rather than prestige, the desire was a mark of devotion.

Where Christians differ: how should the church be governed? Episcopal churches have bishops over priests and deacons (three orders); congregational churches vest final authority in the members; presbyterian churches govern through elders in local sessions and wider courts. Verdict: The New Testament knows two ongoing offices in the local church: elders (overseers), who shepherd, teach and govern, and deacons, who serve practical needs (Philippians 1:1). Each church should be led by a plurality of qualified elders, men who meet these qualifications (Acts 14:23; Titus 1:5). Apostles were a unique, foundational office that has ceased. Within this, churches differ charitably on how much authority the congregation holds and how churches relate to one another.

What it does not mean. It does not mean ambition for position is good. The desire must be for the work, not the power. Nor does it mean the desire alone qualifies someone; the qualifications that follow must be met and tested.

In a sentence. Here is a reliable saying: anyone who sets his heart on being an overseer is longing for a fine work.

On a Tuesday. Pray for your elders by name today. Their work is noble and hard.
verseByVerse.note: “Overseer” and “elder” appear to be two names for the same office.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore an overseer must be above reproach, the husband of one wife, sober-minded, self-controlled, respectable, hospitable, able to teach,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore an overseer must be above reproach, the husband of one wife, sober-minded, self-controlled, respectable, hospitable, able to teach,

Therefore an overseer must be above reproach. Key words. “Must” (dei, it is necessary): these are requirements, not ideals. “Above reproach” (anepilēmptos, not able to be taken hold of, giving no grounds for accusation). This is the headline: the rest of the list explains it. Not sinless, but with no glaring, ongoing pattern of sin that could be fairly charged against him. Notice how little of the list concerns gifts and how much concerns character.

The husband of one wife. Key words. Literally “a one-woman man” (mias gynaikos andra). Several meanings have been proposed: (1) he must not be a polygamist; (2) he must not have remarried after divorce or the death of his wife; (3) he must be married; (4) he must be sexually faithful to his wife, devoted to one woman. The fourth best fits the wording and the context. Polygamy was rare in the Greek world, and Paul encourages remarriage of widows (5:14) and himself was unmarried, so he cannot mean “must be married.” The phrase stresses marital and sexual faithfulness: a man of one woman in heart and conduct.

Sober-minded. Key words. “Sober-minded” (nēphalios, temperate, clear-headed, sometimes used literally of abstinence from wine). Alert, balanced, not given to excess.

Self-controlled. Key words. “Self-controlled” (sōphrōn, sensible, prudent, with sound judgement), a keyword of the Pastoral Letters (2:9, 15; Titus 1:8; 2:2, 5).

Respectable. Key words. “Respectable” (kosmios, orderly, well-behaved, decorous), the same word as 2:9. His life is well-ordered.

Hospitable. Key words. “Hospitable” (philoxenos, a lover of strangers). In the ancient world, travelling Christians depended on the hospitality of believers. An elder’s home is open (Romans 12:13; Hebrews 13:2; 1 Peter 4:9).

Able to teach. Key words. “Able to teach” (didaktikos, skilled in teaching, apt to teach). The one gift-based qualification, and it distinguishes elders from deacons. Elders must be able to explain the truth and refute error (Titus 1:9). Not every elder must be a gifted preacher, but every elder must be able to teach sound doctrine.

Where Christians differ: may a divorced and remarried man be an elder? Some churches forbid it absolutely; others ignore the question. Verdict: The phrase concerns present faithfulness and character, not merely marital history. A man who was divorced on biblical grounds (adultery or desertion by the other spouse, Matthew 19:9; 1 Corinthians 7:15) and has since lived faithfully may be considered. But a man whose divorce was sinful, especially recent, or whose marriage history brings reproach, would not be “above reproach.” Each case requires wise judgement by the church.

What it does not mean. It does not require that elders be married or have children; it describes how they behave if they are. Nor does it describe sinless perfection; it describes mature, consistent Christian character. And these qualities are expected of every Christian; elders must model them.

In a sentence. An overseer, then, must give no grounds for accusation: he must be faithful to his wife, clear-headed, sensible, orderly, open-handed with hospitality, and capable of teaching,

On a Tuesday. Use this list as a mirror for your own life. Which of these qualities does God want to grow in you?

verseByVerse.quote: not a drunkard, not violent but gentle, not quarrelsome, not a lover of money.
verseByVerse.commentary:
not a drunkard, not violent but gentle, not quarrelsome, not a lover of money.

Not a drunkard. Key words. “Drunkard” (paroinos, literally “beside wine,” one who lingers over wine, addicted to it). Drinking wine was normal; drunkenness disqualifies.

Not violent but gentle. Key words. “Violent” (plēktēs, a striker, a bully, quick to use his fists). “Gentle” (epieikēs, gracious, reasonable, forbearing, yielding). An elder deals with people patiently, not harshly (2 Timothy 2:24–25; 1 Peter 5:3).

Not quarrelsome. Key words. “Not quarrelsome” (amachos, not a fighter, peaceable). He does not love argument for its own sake, a pointed requirement given the contentious false teachers (6:4–5).

Not a lover of money. Key words. “Lover of money” (aphilargyros, without love of silver). Greed was a mark of the false teachers (6:5–10; Titus 1:11). Elders may be paid (5:17–18), but they must not be in it for money. The love of money is a root of all kinds of evil (6:10).

What it does not mean. It does not require total abstinence from alcohol; Paul later advises Timothy to drink a little wine (5:23). Nor does “not quarrelsome” mean an elder never contends for the truth; he must refute error (Titus 1:9). The difference is between a contentious spirit and faithful defence of the truth.

In a sentence. not given to heavy drinking, not a bully but gracious, not combative, and not greedy for money.

On a Tuesday. Are you known as gentle? Ask someone close to you, and listen honestly to the answer.

verseByVerse.quote: He must manage his own household well, with all dignity keeping his children submissive, for if someone does not know how to manage his own household, how will he care for God's church?
verseByVerse.commentary:
He must manage his own household well, with all dignity keeping his children submissive, for if someone does not know how to manage his own household, how will he care for God’s church?

He must manage his own household well. Key words. “Manage” (proistēmi, lead, preside over, care for), the same word used of elders who “rule well” (5:17). The household in the ancient world included family, servants and property. A man’s leadership at home is a testing ground for leadership in the church.

With all dignity keeping his children submissive. Key words. “Submissive” (hypotagē, under order, obedient). “With all dignity” (meta pasēs semnotētos) could describe the father’s manner (he leads with dignity, not harshness) or the children’s behaviour (they are respectful). Probably the father: he maintains order in a dignified way, not by shouting or force. This concerns children still at home and under his authority.

For if someone does not know how to manage his own household, how will he care for God’s church? Key words. “Care for” (epimeleomai, take care of, look after), the same word used of the Good Samaritan caring for the wounded man (Luke 10:34–35). Church leadership is not corporate management but tender care. The argument is from lesser to greater: the church is a household (3:15), God’s family. If a man cannot lead his small family well, he will not lead God’s family well.

What it does not mean. It does not mean an elder must have perfect children who never sin, or that he is disqualified because an adult child has chosen to rebel. Children have their own wills. It means his household should show a pattern of godly, loving leadership, and his children at home should generally be respectful and orderly. Nor does it mean an unmarried or childless man cannot be an elder.

In a sentence. He must lead his own family well, keeping his children in order with a dignified manner; after all, if a man does not know how to lead his own family, how can he look after the family of God?

On a Tuesday. Fathers: is your leadership at home marked by dignity and care, or by harshness or neglect? The home is the first place of ministry.

verseByVerse.quote: He must not be a recent convert, or he may become puffed up with conceit and fall into the condemnation of the devil. Moreover, he must be well thought of by outsiders, so that he may not fall into disgrace, into a snare of the devil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He must not be a recent convert, or he may become puffed up with conceit and fall into the condemnation of the devil. Moreover, he must be well thought of by outsiders, so that he may not fall into disgrace, into a snare of the devil.

He must not be a recent convert. Key words. “Recent convert” (neophytos, newly planted; our word “neophyte”). A young believer, however gifted, has not yet been tested or matured. The church at Ephesus was about a dozen years old, so it had mature believers available. (In Crete, a younger church, Paul omits this requirement, Titus 1:5–9.)

Or he may become puffed up with conceit. Key words. “Puffed up” (typhoō, blinded by smoke, wrapped in a fog of pride, conceited). Quick promotion can go to the head.

And fall into the condemnation of the devil. Key words. Two possible meanings: the condemnation the devil received (pride was the devil’s sin, which brought his downfall), or the condemnation the devil brings (accusation by the devil). Most take it as the first: the new convert, swollen with pride, might fall under the same judgement as the devil (Isaiah 14:12–15; Ezekiel 28:17 are often applied to Satan’s fall, though their primary reference is to earthly kings).

Moreover, he must be well thought of by outsiders. Key words. “Well thought of” (martyrian kalēn echein, have a good testimony, good reputation). “Outsiders” (hoi exōthen, those outside the church). The world watches church leaders. A man whom non-Christians know to be dishonest or immoral brings shame on the gospel.

So that he may not fall into disgrace, into a snare of the devil. Key words. “Disgrace” (oneidismos, reproach, insult). “Snare” (pagis, trap). The devil sets traps for leaders, and a poor reputation can be one: accusations, scandal, ruined witness (2 Timothy 2:26).

What it does not mean. It does not mean an elder must be popular with everyone. The world may hate him for the gospel’s sake (John 15:18). It means his conduct should give non-believers no honest grounds for accusation.

In a sentence. He must not be a new believer, or he may be blinded by pride and fall under the devil’s own condemnation; and he must have a good name among those outside the church, so that he does not fall into disgrace and into the devil’s trap.

On a Tuesday. How do your non-Christian neighbours and colleagues see you? Let your daily life make the gospel credible.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Deacons too must be worthy of respect, sincere, not given to much wine or greedy for gain, holding the mystery of the faith with a clear conscience. They should be tested first and serve only if blameless. The women (either deacons’ wives or women deacons) must likewise be dignified, not slanderers, sober and faithful in everything. Deacons should be faithful in marriage and manage their children and households well. Those who serve well gain a good standing and great confidence in their faith in Christ.
verseByVerse.theology:
Wives, or Women Deacons?

The gynaikas of verse 11 may be deacons' wives (so the ESV) or women serving as deacons (cf. Phoebe, Rom 16:1). The passage does not settle it; the standard of character is the same either way.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Missing from the deacons' list is ‘able to teach’: they serve rather than teach, under standards just as demanding.

Now: Test first, then appoint (v.10) — the order most churches reverse, to their cost.

verseByVerse.quote: Deacons likewise must be dignified, not double-tongued, not addicted to much wine, not greedy for dishonest gain. They must hold the mystery of the faith with a clear conscience. And let them also be tested first; then let them serve as deacons if they prove themselves blameless.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Deacons likewise must be dignified, not double-tongued, not addicted to much wine, not greedy for dishonest gain. They must hold the mystery of the faith with a clear conscience. And let them also be tested first; then let them serve as deacons if they prove themselves blameless.

Deacons likewise. Key words. “Deacons” (diakonoi, servants, ministers). The second office. The roots are often traced to Acts 6:1–6, where seven men were chosen to handle the daily distribution of food so the apostles could devote themselves to prayer and the word. Deacons care for the practical and material needs of the church, freeing elders to shepherd and teach. “Likewise”: their character must be as tested as the elders’.

Must be dignified. Key words. “Dignified” (semnos, serious, worthy of respect).

Not double-tongued. Key words. “Double-tongued” (dilogos, saying one thing to one person and another thing to another). Deacons go from house to house; they must be honest and consistent, not gossips or two-faced.

Not addicted to much wine. Key words. Literally “not devoted to much wine.”

Not greedy for dishonest gain. Key words. “Greedy for dishonest gain” (aischrokerdēs, fond of shameful profit). Since deacons handled the church’s money and gifts to the poor, they must be scrupulously honest (compare Judas, John 12:6).

They must hold the mystery of the faith with a clear conscience. Key words. “Mystery” (mystērion, a truth once hidden, now revealed by God). “The faith” is the body of Christian truth. Deacons need not be able to teach (unlike elders), but they must hold sound doctrine firmly and live consistently with it. “A clear conscience” links belief and behaviour (1:5, 19).

And let them also be tested first. Key words. “Tested” (dokimazō, examined, proved, as metal is tested). Not a formal probation necessarily, but an observed track record. The church should know a person’s character before appointing them.

Then let them serve as deacons if they prove themselves blameless. Key words. “Blameless” (anenklētos, unaccused, without charge). Similar to “above reproach” for elders.

What it does not mean. It does not mean deacons are junior elders or that the diaconate is a stepping stone. It is a distinct office of service. Nor does it mean deacons have no spiritual role; Stephen and Philip, among the seven, preached powerfully (Acts 6–8).

In a sentence. In the same way, deacons must be serious people, not two-faced, not given to much wine, not out for shameful profit; they must keep hold of the revealed truth of the faith with a clear conscience. They too should first be tested, and then, if nothing is found against them, they may serve as deacons.

On a Tuesday. Deacons serve quietly. Thank one this week, and ask how you can help them serve.
verseByVerse.note: Deacons (“servants”) cared for the church’s practical needs.

verseByVerse.quote: Their wives likewise must be dignified, not slanderers, but sober-minded, faithful in all things. Let deacons each be the husband of one wife, managing their children and their own households well. For those who serve well as deacons gain a good standing for themselves and also great confidence in the faith that is in Christ Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Their wives likewise must be dignified, not slanderers, but sober-minded, faithful in all things. Let deacons each be the husband of one wife, managing their children and their own households well. For those who serve well as deacons gain a good standing for themselves and also great confidence in the faith that is in Christ Jesus.

Their wives likewise. Key words. The Greek simply says “women” (gynaikas), and can mean either “wives” or “women.” There is no possessive “their.” Two readings: (1) the wives of deacons, who would assist their husbands in ministry; or (2) women deacons (deaconesses). In favour of the second: “likewise” introduces a new group, as with deacons in verse 8; no qualifications are given for elders’ wives, which would be odd if deacons’ wives needed them; and Phoebe is called a diakonos of the church at Cenchreae (Romans 16:1). In favour of the first: verse 12 returns to male deacons as “husbands of one wife,” suggesting the women of verse 11 belong to them. Both views are held by faithful complementarians, since the diaconate is not an office of teaching or governing authority over men.

Must be dignified, not slanderers. Key words. “Dignified” (semnos), as with deacons. “Slanderers” (diaboloi, accusers, malicious gossips; the same word is used of the devil). Women who visit homes and care for needs must not spread what they hear.

But sober-minded, faithful in all things. Key words. “Sober-minded” (nēphalios), as with elders (v. 2). “Faithful in all things” (pistas en pasin, trustworthy in every respect).

Let deacons each be the husband of one wife, managing their children and their own households well. Key words. The same requirements as elders (vv. 2, 4): faithful in marriage, a good leader at home.

For those who serve well as deacons gain a good standing for themselves. Key words. “Good standing” (bathmon kalon, a good step, a good rank, good ground to stand on). Faithful deacons gain respect in the church, and perhaps a good standing before God.

And also great confidence in the faith that is in Christ Jesus. Key words. “Confidence” (parrēsia, boldness, freedom of speech). Faithful service grows assurance and boldness in faith, toward God and in speaking to others.

Where Christians differ: may women serve as deacons? Some say the diaconate is for men only; others allow women deacons. Verdict: Either reading of verse 11 is within faithful bounds. Since deacons do not hold the authority to teach and govern the church (2:12), women may serve in a diaconal capacity, as Phoebe did. Churches should decide wisely and charitably, without treating the question as a test of orthodoxy.

What it does not mean. It does not mean women serving in this way are elders. The teaching and governing office remains limited to qualified men (2:12; 3:2).

In a sentence. In the same way, the women must be serious and respected, not malicious gossips, but clear-headed and dependable in everything. A deacon must be faithful to his wife and lead his children and household well. Those who have served well as deacons win a good standing for themselves and great boldness in the faith that is in Christ Jesus.

On a Tuesday. Guard your tongue this week. Do not repeat what was told you in confidence.
verseByVerse.note: “Their wives” may also be translated “women,” that is, women deacons; the Greek can mean either.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul explains why he is writing: he hopes to visit soon, but if delayed he wants Timothy to know how God’s household should conduct itself, because the church of the living God supports and upholds the truth. And the truth it holds is great. Paul summarises the mystery of the faith in what sounds like an early Christian hymn about Christ: his appearing in human flesh, his vindication by the Spirit, his being seen by angels, his being preached among the nations and believed in the world, and his ascension in glory.
verseByVerse.theology:
Pillar and Buttress

The church does not create the truth; it holds it up where it can be seen (v.15). And the hymn of verse 16 is six passive lines — God does all of it — from ‘manifested in the flesh’ to ‘taken up in glory’.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: In a city of Artemis's hundred-odd columns, house churches are called the pillar of the truth.

Now: The chapter's rules about wine, money and reputation exist so that the pillar stands straight and the mystery of godliness can be seen from the street.

verseByVerse.quote: I hope to come to you soon, but I am writing these things to you so that, if I delay, you may know how one ought to behave in the household of God, which is the church of the living God, a pillar and buttress of the truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I hope to come to you soon, but I am writing these things to you so that, if I delay, you may know how one ought to behave in the household of God, which is the church of the living God, a pillar and buttress of the truth.

I hope to come to you soon, but I am writing these things to you. Key words. Paul hopes to visit, but writes in case he cannot. The letter stands in for his presence, and now stands in for it for the whole church in every generation.

So that, if I delay, you may know how one ought to behave in the household of God. Key words. This verse is the key to the whole letter. “Behave” (anastrephō, conduct oneself, live). “Household” (oikos, house, family). The church is God’s family, with God as Father, believers as brothers and sisters, and elders as stewards (Titus 1:7). It has a proper order and way of life, just as a household does. The instructions about prayer, worship, leaders and widows explain how God’s household should run.

Which is the church of the living God. Key words. “Church” (ekklēsia, assembly, the gathered people). “Of the living God”: in contrast with the dead idols of Ephesus, including the great temple of Artemis (Acts 19:23–41). The true God is alive and present among his people (1 Thessalonians 1:9).

A pillar and buttress of the truth. Key words. “Pillar” (stylos, column, which holds up and displays). “Buttress” (hedraiōma, foundation, support, bulwark). The church holds up the truth for the world to see and holds it firm against attack. Ephesus was famous for the temple of Artemis with its 127 enormous columns. The church is God’s true temple, holding up the truth of the gospel.

Where Christians differ: does the church stand above Scripture? Roman Catholic teaching uses this verse to argue that the church, through its teaching office, is the infallible guardian and interpreter of truth, and that Scripture and tradition together form the rule of faith. Verdict: The church supports the truth; it does not create it or stand over it. The truth is God’s Word, which the church receives, guards, and proclaims (2 Timothy 1:13–14; Jude 3). When a church departs from Scripture, it ceases to be a pillar of truth, as the false teachers in Ephesus showed. Scripture alone is the final authority over the church (sola Scriptura).

What it does not mean. It does not mean the church is a building. The household is people. Nor does it mean the church is the source of truth; Christ and his Word are.

In a sentence. I hope to visit you soon, but I am writing this in case I am held up, so that you will know how people are to conduct themselves in God’s household, which is the assembly of the living God, the column and support that holds up the truth.

For worship. Thank God for your local church, imperfect as it is: it is the household of the living God and holds up his truth in your town.

verseByVerse.quote: Great indeed, we confess, is the mystery of godliness: He was manifested in the flesh, vindicated by the Spirit, seen by angels, proclaimed among the nations, believed on in the world, taken up in glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Great indeed, we confess, is the mystery of godliness: He was manifested in the flesh, vindicated by the Spirit, seen by angels, proclaimed among the nations, believed on in the world, taken up in glory.

Great indeed, we confess, is the mystery of godliness. Key words. “We confess” (homologoumenōs, by common confession, undeniably, as all agree). Paul introduces what the whole church confesses. “Mystery” (mystērion): a truth hidden in the past and now revealed. “Of godliness” (tēs eusebeias): the truth that produces godliness, the revealed secret at the heart of true religion. Perhaps a deliberate contrast with the Ephesian cry, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!” (Acts 19:28, 34).

He was manifested in the flesh. Key words. The truth at the centre of godliness is a person: Christ. “He” (hos, who). “Manifested” (phaneroō, made visible, revealed). “In the flesh”: in true human nature. This assumes his pre-existence: he existed before he was made visible. The incarnation (John 1:14).

Vindicated by the Spirit. Key words. “Vindicated” (dikaioō, declared righteous, justified, shown to be in the right). Rejected and crucified as a criminal, he was declared righteous and the Son of God by the Spirit in his resurrection (Romans 1:4; 1 Peter 3:18). Or “in the spirit,” in the realm of the Spirit, the new life of resurrection.

Seen by angels. Key words. Angels witnessed his resurrection and ascension (Matthew 28:2–7; Acts 1:10–11), and perhaps the whole of his triumphant entry into heaven (Ephesians 1:20–21; 1 Peter 3:22).

Proclaimed among the nations. Key words. “Proclaimed” (kēryssō, heralded). “Nations” (ethnesin, Gentiles). The message went to the whole world, picking up 2:4–7.

Believed on in the world. Key words. Not merely proclaimed but believed. People across the world have trusted him.

Taken up in glory. Key words. “Taken up” (analambanō), the word used of the ascension (Acts 1:2, 11, 22). He now reigns in glory at the Father’s right hand.

Setting and background. This is probably an early Christian hymn or creed. It has six lines, each beginning with a verb in the same form, arranged perhaps in three pairs that contrast earth and heaven: flesh/Spirit, angels/nations, world/glory. The movement is from the incarnation to the exaltation.

Textual note. Many later manuscripts (followed by the KJV) read “God was manifest in the flesh” (theos) instead of “He who was manifested” (hos). In ancient manuscripts, the abbreviation for “God” (ΘΣ) looked very like “who” (ΟΣ) with a small line added. The earliest and best manuscripts read “who,” and this is the more likely original. The deity of Christ does not depend on this verse; it is clearly taught elsewhere (John 1:1; Romans 9:5; Titus 2:13; Hebrews 1:8), and the hymn itself assumes his pre-existence.

What it does not mean. It does not mean “mystery” is something unknowable or puzzling. It is a revealed secret, now openly confessed. Nor is godliness a technique; it is the fruit of knowing Christ.

In a sentence. Beyond all doubt, great is the revealed secret from which godliness springs: he appeared in a human body, was proved right by the Spirit, was seen by angels, was announced among the nations, was trusted throughout the world, and was taken up into glory.

For worship. Read or sing this hymn aloud. Then praise Christ for each line: his incarnation, resurrection, triumph, mission, saving power and reign.
verseByVerse.note: Probably an early Christian hymn or creed, with six lines in three pairs. “He” is literally “Who” in Greek; some manuscripts read “God,” others “Which” (ESV note).

4.title: A Good Servant of Christ Jesus
4.overview:
The Spirit has warned that some will abandon the faith, following teachers whose consciences are seared and who forbid marriage and certain foods. Paul answers with creation: everything God made is good and to be received with thanks, made holy by God’s word and prayer.

Then he turns to Timothy. Refuse silly myths and train yourself for godliness, which, unlike bodily training, pays out in this life and the next. Do not let anyone despise your youth; be an example in speech, conduct, love, faith and purity. Give yourself to the public reading of Scripture, to exhortation and to teaching. Let your progress be seen. Watch your life and your doctrine closely, for in this way God will save you and your hearers.

verseByVerse.ref: 4:1–5 – Some Will Depart from the Faith
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Spirit has warned that in the last times some will desert the faith, drawn by deceiving spirits and teaching that comes from demons, spread by hypocrites whose consciences have been burned numb. These teachers forbid marriage and ban certain foods, though God made food to be eaten gratefully by believers who know the truth. Paul insists that everything God created is good and nothing should be refused if it is received with thanks, because God’s word and prayer make it holy.
verseByVerse.theology:
False Teaching That Restricts Rather Than Permits

The Ephesian error was ascetic — impressive for what it gave up — and Paul answers it not by negotiating but with Genesis 1: everything God made is good, created to be received with thanksgiving (vv.3–4).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Seared consciences are made one over-ruling at a time, through ordinary men saying what they know to be untrue (v.2).

Now: Grace at the table sanctifies a common meal (v.5): neither refuse the gift nor grab it, but take it and say thank you.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the Spirit expressly says that in later times some will depart from the faith by devoting themselves to deceitful spirits and teachings of demons, through the insincerity of liars whose consciences are seared,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Spirit warns that some will depart from the faith, following deceitful spirits and teachings of demons.

Expressly. In so many words: a revealed warning, perhaps through prophets or Jesus’ own teaching.

Later times. Already begun. Paul describes Ephesus.

Demons behind it. False teaching is not merely a clever man reasoning badly; there is a source behind the visible one.

Through ordinary liars. No spectacle. Men saying what they know is untrue, in a normal voice, at a meeting.

Seared. Branded. Scar tissue does not feel. A conscience is deadened one small over-ruling at a time (1:19), and at the end it does not hurt.

On a Tuesday. If something you once felt guilty about no longer bothers you, ask whether you changed your mind or your nerve died.

verseByVerse.quote: who forbid marriage and require abstinence from foods that God created to be received with thanksgiving by those who believe and know the truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They forbid marriage and certain foods that God created to be received with thanksgiving.

Restriction, not licence. We expect false teaching to be permissive. This was ascetic, impressive for what it gave up. That has been at least as common in church history.

Behind it. The idea that matter is the problem and holiness means escaping the body (compare Colossians 2:21). Marriage and food, the most bodily things, had to go.

God created. Paul goes straight to creation. Refusing the gift is not superior spirituality; it insults the Giver. They were made to be received.

Clerical celibacy? The Reformers applied this verse to compulsory celibacy for priests. Singleness freely chosen for the kingdom is good (Matthew 19:12; 1 Corinthians 7:7). A rule forbidding ministers to marry is not. Likewise, a Christian may avoid meat for health or conscience; teaching that holiness requires it is wrong.

Those who know the truth. Unbelievers eat and marry; they cannot receive them as gifts, because they do not know whom to thank.

verseByVerse.quote: For everything created by God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving, for it is made holy by the word of God and prayer.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everything God created is good, and is made holy by his word and prayer.

Good. Genesis 1’s verdict, never withdrawn. The fall damaged the world’s use, not its origin.

What it does not mean. Not that anything goes. Paul speaks of created gifts such as food and marriage, not of sin. Drunkenness misuses wine; adultery misuses sex.

With thanksgiving. Gratitude turns eating into worship. The line is not between things but between ways of receiving them.

The word of God and prayer. Probably Scripture’s verdict that it is good, and grace before meals.

Saying grace. The most routine Christian habit, done on autopilot, is given priestly weight. It sets a common meal apart.

On a Tuesday. Neither refuse the gift nor grab it. Take it and say thank you, at the very moment you are most likely to forget God: when you are enjoying something.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: By teaching these things Timothy will be a good servant of Christ, nourished on the faith and sound teaching he has followed. He must reject silly myths and train himself for godliness, which is of value in every way, holding promise for this life and the next, unlike mere physical training. This is why Christians labour and struggle: their hope is in the living God, the Saviour of all people, especially of those who believe. Timothy should not let anyone despise his youth, but set an example in speech, conduct, love, faith and purity, devote himself to the public reading of Scripture, preaching and teaching, and not neglect the gift given him when the elders laid hands on him. Watching his life and doctrine closely, he will save both himself and his hearers.
verseByVerse.theology:
Godliness Is Trained For

Godliness is trained for like a body, by repetition (v.7), and unlike bodily training its results survive the body — with value for this life as well as the next (v.8). God is Saviour of all as their preserver, and especially of believers (v.10).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Public reading of Scripture came first (v.13) in a church where few could read: read, explain, apply.

Now: A young leader earns respect by being an example where nobody is watching (v.12), and a minister whose progress is visible (v.15) teaches his people that growth does not stop.

verseByVerse.quote: If you put these things before the brothers, you will be a good servant of Christ Jesus, being trained in the words of the faith and of the good doctrine that you have followed. Have nothing to do with irreverent, silly myths. Rather train yourself for godliness;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Timothy will be a good servant by teaching these truths and training himself in godliness, not myths.

A good servant. Diakonos. Not by innovating, but by serving up what he was given.

Being nourished. Present tense. A minister who stops being fed will soon have nothing to serve.

Old-womanish myths. Deliberately dismissive. Some error deserves careful answer; some deserves to be walked past. Arguing can concede that a thing is worth arguing about.

Train. Gymnaze, the gymnasium word. Godliness is not a temperament some are born with; it is trained for by repeating unremarkable things long after they stop being interesting.

On a Tuesday. Pick one spiritual discipline (a set time of prayer, a Bible plan, a weekly fast) and keep at it when you do not feel like it.

verseByVerse.quote: for while bodily training is of some value, godliness is of value in every way, as it holds promise for the present life and also for the life to come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Bodily training has some value, but godliness is valuable in every way, now and for eternity.

Some value. A real concession. Paul has just defended food and marriage; he does not despise the body. Go to the gym.

Scope. Bodily training helps a little, for a while. Even the strongest body is on a schedule. Godliness is the only training whose results outlast the body.

This life too. Not a religion that pays only after death. Self-control beats being ruled by appetite; a clear conscience sleeps better; love is better company than resentment.

What it does not mean. Not that godliness brings wealth (6:5). Its present value is a better life, not a richer one.

Encouragement. Nobody changes a body by one decision. The soul works the same way. Progress does not depend on inspiration.

verseByVerse.quote: The saying is trustworthy and deserving of full acceptance. For to this end we toil and strive, because we have our hope set on the living God, who is the Savior of all people, especially of those who believe.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Believers labour because their hope is set on the living God, the Saviour of all, especially of believers.

Toil and strive. Labour to exhaustion; contend in the arena. Paul puts himself in the gym.

Hope, not duty. The fuel is expectation, in a God who is alive, unlike Artemis down the road.

Saviour of all? Not universal salvation; the chapter opened with people abandoning the faith. Some read “all kinds of people” again. The likelier sense uses the breadth of “saviour”: God preserves and sustains every living person (Matthew 5:45; Acts 17:25), and in the full and eternal sense saves those who believe.

One generosity, two depths. Fitting after Paul’s defence of creation: the God who feeds everyone is the God who saves believers.

For worship. Every breath an unbeliever draws is a mercy from the God he ignores. So is yours.

verseByVerse.quote: Command and teach these things. Let no one despise you for your youth, but set the believers an example in speech, in conduct, in love, in faith, in purity.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Timothy must teach with authority and set an example in speech, conduct, love, faith and purity, whatever his youth.

Command. Stronger than suggest, because the instructions were never Timothy’s own.

Youth. Probably in his thirties: young in a culture that gave authority to age, with older men who wanted his role.

Not “assert yourself”. Paul does not tell him to fight for respect, or the church to give it. He tells him to give contempt nothing to feed on.

Example. Typos, the stamp. Authority displayed, not claimed.

Five areas. From the most visible (speech) to the least (purity), and the least visible is where it is decided.

On a Tuesday. Young Christians: you do not need to be older to be an example. Older Christians: do not despise the young leader whose life is worth copying.
verseByVerse.note: Timothy was probably in his thirties — young for a church leader in that culture.

verseByVerse.quote: Until I come, devote yourself to the public reading of Scripture, to exhortation, to teaching. Do not neglect the gift you have, which was given you by prophecy when the council of elders laid their hands on you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He must devote himself to the public reading of Scripture, exhortation and teaching, using his gift.

Public reading first. Most could not read, and copies were scarce. Hearing the Bible meant someone reading it aloud. Before explanation, the text itself.

Read, exhort, teach. Read, apply, explain: Christian ministry in three words.

On a Tuesday. If your church reads only a verse or two before the sermon, ask whether it could read more. Scripture read aloud is itself ministry.

Do not neglect. A gift can be possessed and wasted, left in a drawer.

The laying on of hands. The elders publicly recognised and set Timothy apart for a gift the Spirit had given. Roman Catholic and Orthodox teaching regards ordination as a sacrament conveying grace. Here the act recognises and commissions; the gift is the Spirit’s.

A council. Plural. When the job goes badly, remember that a body of men publicly stood with you.

verseByVerse.quote: Practice these things, immerse yourself in them, so that all may see your progress. Keep a close watch on yourself and on the teaching. Persist in this, for by so doing you will save both yourself and your hearers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He must practise these things and keep close watch on himself and his teaching, for in this he will save himself and his hearers.

Immerse yourself. Literally “be in these things”. Live there.

Progress. Prokopē, cutting a road ahead. Visible: the congregation should see a better man than five years ago. A leader who never visibly grows teaches that growth stops.

Yourself first. Then the teaching. A man can guard his theology while his character comes apart (1:19). But both: character without sound teaching helps no one; sound teaching from a corrupt man is a weapon.

Save yourself and your hearers. No minister saves anyone; there is one mediator (2:5). God saves through means, including a man who keeps watching himself and teaching truly. Perseverance in faith is how salvation is kept, by God’s power.

On a Tuesday. Watch yourself: what you read, watch and think about when no one is checking.

4.text: <sup>1</sup>Now the Spirit expressly says that in later times some will depart from the faith by devoting themselves to deceitful spirits and teachings of demons,<sup>2</sup>through the insincerity of liars whose consciences are seared,<sup>3</sup>who forbid marriage and require abstinence from foods that God created to be received with thanksgiving by those who believe and know the truth.<sup>4</sup>For everything created by God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving,<sup>5</sup>for it is made holy by the word of God and prayer.<sup>6</sup>If you put these things before the brothers, you will be a good servant of Christ Jesus, being trained in the words of the faith and of the good doctrine that you have followed.<sup>7</sup>Have nothing to do with irreverent, silly myths. Rather train yourself for godliness;<sup>8</sup>for while bodily training is of some value, godliness is of value in every way, as it holds promise for the present life and also for the life to come.<sup>9</sup>The saying is trustworthy and deserving of full acceptance.<sup>10</sup>For to this end we toil and strive, because we have our hope set on the living God, who is the Savior of all people, especially of those who believe.<sup>11</sup>Command and teach these things.<sup>12</sup>Let no one despise you for your youth, but set the believers an example in speech, in conduct, in love, in faith, in purity.<sup>13</sup>Until I come, devote yourself to the public reading of Scripture, to exhortation, to teaching.<sup>14</sup>Do not neglect the gift you have, which was given you by prophecy when the council of elders laid their hands on you.<sup>15</sup>Practice these things, immerse yourself in them, so that all may see your progress.<sup>16</sup>Keep a close watch on yourself and on the teaching. 5.title: Honour and Order in the Family of God
5.overview:
The church is a family, and Paul tells Timothy how to treat its members: older men as fathers, younger men as brothers, older women as mothers, younger women as sisters, in all purity. Then two practical matters. Widows: the church must support those truly alone, but families must first care for their own, and a Christian who neglects his relatives “has denied the faith”. Younger widows should remarry rather than take a vow they may not keep.

Elders: those who lead well, especially in preaching, should be paid generously, and Paul quotes a saying of Jesus as Scripture. Accusations against elders need two or three witnesses, but elders who persist in sin are rebuked publicly. Appoint slowly, judge without favouritism, and remember that both hidden sins and hidden goodness will come to light.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Timothy is to treat the congregation like family. He should not scold an older man but appeal to him respectfully as he would to his own father, and treat younger men as brothers, older women as mothers, and younger women as sisters, with complete purity.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Church as Household, in Practice

This is 3:15 turned into method: treat people as what they actually are — fathers, brothers, mothers, sisters — which rules out both harshness and a deference that never says anything.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A young leader not taken seriously is tempted to be harsher than the case requires (4:12).

Now: ‘As sisters, in all purity’ gives a relationship rather than a rulebook as the safeguard.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not rebuke an older man but encourage him as you would a father, younger men as brothers, older women as mothers, younger women as sisters, in all purity.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Timothy must treat church members as family: older men as fathers, younger men as brothers, women with purity.

Not harshly. To strike with words. Older men may need correcting, but not like that. A young leader not taken seriously (4:12) is tempted to compensate by being sharper than the case needs.

A family. The church as God’s household (3:15), in practice. You correct your father carefully and never in public; you are frank with a brother. It rules out both harshness and a deference that never says anything.

In all purity. Added only for younger women. A realist’s word to a young unmarried minister: many ministries have been destroyed here.

As sisters. The safeguard is a relationship, not a rulebook. A man already knows what is unthinkable with his sister. It protects them both without treating half the church as a hazard.

On a Tuesday. Think of the hardest person in your church. How would you speak to them if they were family? They are.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The church should honour and support widows who are truly alone and in need. Families must first care for their own widowed relatives; anyone who fails to provide for his own household has denied the faith. A true widow hopes in God and gives herself to prayer, while one who lives for pleasure is dead even while she lives. Paul sets out who may be enrolled for church support: widows over sixty, faithful in marriage and known for good works such as raising children, hospitality and serving others. Younger widows should rather marry, bring up children and manage a home, giving the enemy no opportunity, since some have already strayed. Believing women with widows in the family should support them, so that the church can help those truly in need.
verseByVerse.theology:
Family First, and Why

To neglect one's own relatives is to deny the faith and fall below the decency of unbelievers (v.8); caring for an ageing parent is not a lesser duty but where godliness is practised (v.4).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The enrolled widows were intercessors (v.5), and their credentials were a lifetime of unrecorded service (v.10).

Now: Paul's remedy for the dangers of verses 11–13 is not more restriction but ordinary life (v.14).

verseByVerse.quote: Honor widows who are truly widows. But if a widow has children or grandchildren, let them first learn to show godliness to their own household and to make some return to their parents, for this is pleasing in the sight of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The church should honour widows truly in need, but families must care for their own first.

Honour. Including money, as in v. 17. This is the church’s welfare list.

A widow then. No state support, few respectable ways to earn, often no property. Without family she was destitute. God defends the widow (Deuteronomy 10:18); the church’s first crisis was about widows (Acts 6:1).

Truly widows. Limited funds must reach the genuinely alone.

Family first. The church is not the first line of support. Children repay a debt.

Where godliness is. Caring for an ageing mother is not a secular duty keeping you from spiritual things. It is godliness. The opposite of the “Corban” dodge Jesus condemned (Mark 7:9–13).

On a Tuesday. Phone your parents. If they are old, ask what they need.

verseByVerse.quote: She who is truly a widow, left all alone, has set her hope on God and continues in supplications and prayers night and day, but she who is self-indulgent is dead even while she lives.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The true widow hopes in God and continues in prayer; self-indulgence is spiritual death.

Alone. Not only bereaved but with no one to turn to.

Night and day. Like Anna in the temple (Luke 2:37). The church is not only giving charity; it is supporting intercessors. A congregation that keeps its widows is buying prayer it could not otherwise afford.

Self-indulgent. Resources, no dependants, freedom spent on pleasure.

Dead while she lives. Present tense, like Sardis (Revelation 3:1).

Two women. Both widowed, both with time. One prays and is alive; the other spends it on herself and has not noticed she is dead.

On a Tuesday. Retired? What you do with unstructured time reveals you. Spend some of it praying for your church.

verseByVerse.quote: Command these things as well, so that they may be without reproach. But if anyone does not provide for his relatives, and especially for members of his household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Anyone who does not provide for his relatives has denied the faith.

Without reproach. The overseer’s word (3:2), now for families caring for their own. A watching city judges Christian homes.

Denied the faith. Peter’s verb in the courtyard. A man can recite the creed and, by leaving his mother destitute, deny every word.

Worse than an unbeliever. Pagans looked after their own. Neglect falls below ordinary decency.

What it does not mean. It does not settle every hard case: estrangement for grave reasons, relatives no money can help, carers at the end of their strength. Paul means those who could and do not, and have arranged their religion so as not to notice.

On a Tuesday. Spirituality here is measured not by devotion or ministry, but by whether your relatives have what they need.

verseByVerse.quote: Let a widow be enrolled if she is not less than sixty years of age, having been the wife of one husband, and having a reputation for good works: if she has brought up children, has shown hospitality, has washed the feet of the saints, has cared for the afflicted, and has devoted herself to every good work.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Only older widows of proven godliness should be enrolled for the church’s support.

Enrolled. An official list, probably with duties.

Sixty. Past likely remarriage and earning: where long-term dependence begins.

Wife of one husband. A faithful wife. Not excluding remarriage after widowhood, since Paul urges younger widows to remarry (v. 14).

Washed feet. The lowest household job, which Jesus did (John 13:5).

Unrecorded credentials. Not one item is public. She is enrolled for a lifetime of things nobody wrote down. Before she needed help, she gave it.

On a Tuesday. The church owes its quiet servants. Find out who in your church is now in need after years of helping others.
verseByVerse.note: There seems to have been an official list of widows supported by the church, who in turn served it.

verseByVerse.quote: But refuse to enroll younger widows, for when their passions draw them away from Christ, they desire to marry and so incur condemnation for having abandoned their former faith. Besides that, they learn to be idlers, going about from house to house, and not only idlers, but also gossips and busybodies, saying what they should not.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Younger widows should not be enrolled, for they may break their pledge and fall into idleness.

Not against remarriage. Paul urges it in v. 14.

Their former pledge. Most likely a commitment made on joining the list, to remain unmarried in the church’s service. Breaking it is the problem, not marrying.

Pastoral realism. Do not ask a woman in her twenties to bind herself for life. Most will not manage it, and the failure will damage them.

They learn. The arrangement teaches it. A stipend with no work or structure fills days somehow, often with other people’s business (2 Thessalonians 3:11).

The general lesson. Not about women or widows. Idleness is never neutral. Remove someone’s proper work and the energy goes into other people’s affairs.

verseByVerse.quote: So I would have younger widows marry, bear children, manage their households, and give the adversary no occasion for slander. For some have already strayed after Satan. If any believing woman has relatives who are widows, let her care for them. Let the church not be burdened, so that it may care for those who are truly widows.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Younger widows should marry and manage their homes, and families should support their own widows.

Marry. Not only allowed; preferred. Against teachers who forbade marriage (4:3), Paul’s cure is ordinary life.

Manage their households. Literally “rule the house”: a real sphere of authority.

No occasion. The church is watched from the street (3:7).

Already. Not hypothetical. Some had gone off the road.

The arithmetic of love. Every family that supports its own frees the church to help those with no one.

A textual note. Many later manuscripts read “any believing man or woman” (KJV). The shorter “believing woman” is earlier, and harder, so more likely original. The duty of v. 8 is not men’s alone.

Today. Few churches keep a widows’ list, but the principle stands: real need, met first by family, then by the church. Families may not hand their duty to the church or the state.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Elders who lead well deserve double honour, especially those who labour at preaching and teaching, for Scripture says a working ox is not to be muzzled and the worker deserves his wages. An accusation against an elder must be backed by two or three witnesses; those who persist in sin are to be rebuked publicly, as a warning to others. Timothy must apply these instructions without prejudice or favouritism, and must not be hasty in laying hands on anyone or share in others’ sins. Paul adds a personal word: he should drink a little wine for his frequent stomach trouble. Some people’s sins and good deeds are obvious; others come to light later, but none remain hidden.
verseByVerse.theology:
A Gospel Quoted as Scripture

Verse 18 introduces both Deuteronomy 25:4 and a saying of Jesus recorded at Luke 10:7 with ‘the Scripture says’ — among the earliest signs that the written words of Jesus were already counted as Scripture.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Elders are hard to accuse (v.19) and hard to hide behind (v.20); a church needs both verses.

Now: Verse 23 shows Paul correcting a good man's over-scrupulous mistake, and verse 25 promises that unrecorded goodness cannot stay hidden.

verseByVerse.quote: Let the elders who rule well be considered worthy of double honor, especially those who labor in preaching and teaching. For the Scripture says, "You shall not muzzle an ox when it treads out the grain," and, "The laborer deserves his wages."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Elders who rule well, especially in preaching and teaching, deserve double honour, including pay.

Honour means pay. Both quotations are about paying workers.

Double. Generous, not grudging.

Especially. Implies some elders taught and some did not. Presbyterians see here teaching and ruling elders; Baptists and others usually see one office with differing labours. The text allows either.

Labour. Kopiaō, work to exhaustion. Preaching is not restful.

The ox. Deuteronomy 25:4, applied to people (1 Corinthians 9:9).

“The Scripture says.” The second quotation is Jesus’ saying in Luke 10:7. Paul calls both Scripture: one of the earliest signs that Jesus’ written words already stood with the Old Testament (compare 2 Peter 3:16).

On a Tuesday. Is your church paying its pastor enough to live without anxiety? Ask.
verseByVerse.note: The two sayings come from Deuteronomy and from Jesus’ words as recorded in Luke — a sign that the Gospels were already being received as Scripture.

parallels.desc: You shall not muzzle an ox when it is treading out the grain

verseByVerse.quote: Do not admit a charge against an elder except on the evidence of two or three witnesses. As for those who persist in sin, rebuke them in the presence of all, so that the rest may stand in fear.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Accusations against elders need two or three witnesses, and those who persist in sin must be rebuked publicly.

Two or three witnesses. Deuteronomy 19:15; Matthew 18:16. A public man is a target; accusations cost the accuser nothing. Do not even open proceedings on one person’s word.

Not a shield. Those who persist, after private dealing, are rebuked publicly.

Against instinct. Churches usually protect the institution: settle quietly, move the man on. Paul says public office, public correction, so others fear.

Both verses. Hard to accuse; hard to hide behind. Keep only the first and leaders become untouchable; keep only the second and any grievance ruins a man.

What it does not mean. The witness rule is about church discipline. It never means a church may ignore a crime or refuse to report abuse to the authorities.

parallels.desc: on the evidence of two witnesses or of three witnesses

verseByVerse.quote: In the presence of God and of Christ Jesus and of the elect angels I charge you to keep these rules without prejudging, doing nothing from partiality.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Timothy must apply these instructions without partiality.

Sworn in. The most solemn sentence in the letter.

Elect angels. Watchers of church life (1 Corinthians 11:10; 1 Peter 1:12), distinguished from the fallen. A courtroom with an unseen gallery.

Prejudging, partiality. Deciding in advance; leaning one way. Timothy will have friends and opponents among the elders, and will know before hearing a charge which way he wants it to go.

The test. Rules are easy when the accused is a stranger. The hard case is when you already know whose side you are on. Paul’s answer is not better procedure, but who is watching.

On a Tuesday. In any dispute (at work, in your family), notice who you want to be right before you hear the facts.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not be hasty in the laying on of hands, nor take part in the sins of others; keep yourself pure.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He must not ordain anyone hastily, and must keep himself pure.

Laying on of hands. Appointment to office (4:14).

Do not be hasty. As at 3:6. Ephesus needed leaders, and the pressure to fill posts was great.

Share in sins. Whoever appoints carelessly is implicated in what the appointed man later does. He cannot say he could not have known, since testing (3:10) would often have shown him.

Keep yourself pure. A great deal of holiness is kept or lost in decisions that look merely procedural.

On a Tuesday. Writing a reference or recommending someone? You share responsibility. Be honest.

verseByVerse.quote: No longer drink only water, but use a little wine for the sake of your stomach and your frequent ailments.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Timothy should take a little wine for his health.

A window into a friendship. Medical advice in the middle of instructions on discipline.

Two facts. Timothy was often ill, and he drank only water, risky when supplies were unsafe and wine was used to purify them.

Why? Probably on principle: against ascetics (4:3), and wanting to be above reproach (3:3), he went teetotal and made himself ill.

A little, for your stomach. Neither a licence nor a prohibition.

Why not heal him? Even Paul, through whom God did extraordinary miracles (Acts 19:11–12), did not heal at will, and here prescribes a remedy. Illness is not always a sign of sin or weak faith, and using medicine is no lack of trust.

For the scrupulous. A good man’s mistake: trying to be blameless and overshooting into harm. Paul does not praise the rigour. He tells him to stop.

verseByVerse.quote: The sins of some people are conspicuous, going before them to judgment, but the sins of others appear later. So also good works are conspicuous, and even those that are not cannot remain hidden.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some sins and good works are obvious, others come to light later; none stays hidden.

Conspicuous sins. They walk ahead like heralds; no examination needed.

Later. Others catch up eventually.

Honest. After careful procedure (3:10; 5:19, 22), Paul admits it will not catch everything. He does not respond by adding more rules.

Nothing stays hidden. If not now, then at judgment. So haste is unnecessary: waiting does not risk the truth never emerging.

The kinder half. The same law runs for goodness. The widow’s unrecorded lifetime (v. 10) is not lost.

On a Tuesday. If your faithfulness has gone unnoticed, or someone else got the credit, both ledgers are being kept, and both will be read out.
